extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, and students of English composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for producing clear, concise, and correct English prose, including principles of sentence construction, punctuation, formatting, and commonly misused words/phrases. Suitable for writers preparing manuscripts, essays, summaries, and formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words
rubrics_metrics.description: Make every word tell; avoid unnecessary words and phrases that add nothing to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace verbose expressions (e.g., 'the question as to whether' → 'whether'; 'the fact that' → delete or recast). Prefer concise phrasings such as 'my arrival' instead of 'the fact that I had arrived.' See numerous examples of superfluous phrases and how to shorten or recast them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer positive statements and active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive statement is more concise than a negative; the active voice is more concise than the passive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use affirmative constructions and active verbs where appropriate. Examples illustrate compressing several short sentences into a single concise active sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a succession of loose sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not produce a series of similarly structured loose sentences (two co-ordinate clauses, second introduced by a conjunction or relative), which becomes monotonous and tedious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace some sentences with simple sentences, semicolon-joined clauses, periodic sentences, or sentences of varied clause count to remove mechanical symmetry and monotony. Examples compare weak paragraph of repetitive loose sentences with stronger varied prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form (parallel construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of similar content and function should be outwardly similar in form to help the reader recognize likeness of content and function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parallel grammatical constructions for lists, correlative expressions (both...and, not only...but also, either...or, first, second...), and series. Examples show corrections (e.g., 'Formerly, science was taught by the textbook method; now it is taught by the laboratory method'). For many similar items, group them or use a table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep related words together
rubrics_metrics.description: Position words and groups of words so that those related in thought are close together and unrelated elements are kept apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid separating subject and principal verb with transferrable phrases or clauses; place relative pronoun immediately after antecedent; arrange modifiers next to the words they modify to prevent wrong relations. Exceptions: deliberate periodic sentences or appositive/relative clauses where no ambiguity occurs. Examples demonstrating corrections and acceptable exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: In summaries, keep to one tense
rubrics_metrics.description: When summarizing, use a single tense consistently: present tense for drama and preferably for poems/stories (past allowed), with antecedent actions in the perfect or past perfect as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid shifting tenses, which suggests uncertainty. Use present/perfect or past/past-perfect consistently. Indicate once at the outset when the following is a summary and avoid repeated introductory phrases like 'he said' throughout the summary. In criticism/interpretation avoid turning into mere summary; aim for orderly discussion supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the emphatic words at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: The most prominent (emphatic) word or group of words in a sentence should usually come at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The logical predicate (new element) often deserves the end position. Periodic sentences gain prominence from putting the main statement at the end. The sentence beginning can also be emphatic, but subject alone rarely attains strong emphasis there. Apply the principle to words in sentences, sentences in paragraphs, and paragraphs in compositions. Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headings (manuscript formatting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave a blank line after the title or heading of a manuscript. On succeeding pages, if using ruled paper, begin on the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple formatting rule for manuscript headings and pagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals (dates and serial numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not spell out dates or other serial numbers; write them in figures or Roman notation as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'August 9, 1918' (or '9 August 1918'); 'Rule 3', 'Chapter XII', '352nd Infantry'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses (punctuation rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuate a sentence containing a parenthetical expression as if the expression were absent; punctuate the parenthetical expression as if it stood alone except omit the final full stop unless it's a question or exclamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate commas and placement of final punctuation for wholly detached parenthetical sentences. E.g., 'I went to his house yesterday (my third attempt to see him), but he had left town.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations (punctuation and formatting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal documentary quotations are introduced by a colon and enclosed in quotation marks; quotations in apposition or as direct objects are preceded by a comma; long verse lines begin on a fresh centered line without quotation marks; quotations introduced by 'that' are indirect and not enclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: constitutional provision with colon and quotes; appositional quotations with comma; treatment of verse and proverbial phrases; colloquialisms and slang need no quotation marks when established.

rubrics_metrics.name: References (scholarly citation practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: In scholarly work give exact references; abbreviate frequently occurring titles, give full forms in an alphabetical list at the end, and as a general practice give references in parenthesis or footnotes rather than in the running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit words like act, scene, line, book, volume, page when possible. Examples of play/verse citation formats and biblical citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllabication (hyphenation at line breaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: If only part of a word fits at the end of a line, divide the word according to formation, 'on the vowel', between double letters with exceptions, and avoid dividing before a final silent '-ed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide many examples of acceptable hyphenation patterns and encourage checking printed books for practice; no absolute rule for all words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles (formatting of literary works)
rubrics_metrics.description: For titles of literary works, scholarly usage prefers italics with capitalized initials; omit initial 'A' or 'The' from titles when placing the possessive before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use italics except when writing for a periodical with a different practice. Examples: The Iliad; As You Like It; Dickens's Tale of Two Cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words and expressions commonly misused — general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of frequently misused words/phrases; the writer should aim to express accurately rather than rely on ready-made formulas, recasting sentences when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefatory note: some listed forms are outright bad, some debatable (split infinitive), some good in place but overused. When accidentally used, the preferred course is often to recast the sentence rather than substitute single words.

rubrics_metrics.name: All right
rubrics_metrics.description: Idiomatic in familiar speech as a detached phrase meaning 'Agreed' or 'Go ahead'; in other uses better avoided; always written as two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cautiously in writing; treat as informal.

rubrics_metrics.name: As good or better than
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid constructions like 'My opinion is as good or better than his'; correct by rearrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'My opinion is as good as his' or 'My opinion is better than his' (if better).

rubrics_metrics.name: As to whether
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'whether' alone; 'as to whether' is redundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Rule 13 on omitting needless words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bid (verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Takes the infinitive without 'to'; past tense meaning 'ordered' is 'bade'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct infinitive construction and past tense form.

rubrics_metrics.name: But (overuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'But' is unnecessary after 'doubt' and 'help'; excessive use leads to loose sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like 'I have no doubt but that' → 'I have no doubt that'; replace 'help see but that' with 'help seeing that'. Avoid chaining 'but' to contrast contrasts; rearrange sentences to remove successive 'but's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Can (ability vs permission)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Can' means 'am/is/are able' and should not be used as a substitute for 'may'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'may' for permission, 'can' for ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case (unnecessary use)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'case' in senses like 'instance' or 'usual state of affairs' is often unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct phrasing: 'Many of the rooms were poorly ventilated' rather than 'In many cases, the rooms were poorly ventilated.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainly (overused intensifier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Used indiscriminately as an intensifier, like an empty 'very'; bad in speech and worse in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid habitual use to intensify statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (redundant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often redundant when combined with 'acts' or other nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Hostile acts' instead of 'Acts of a hostile character'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim (verb usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: With an object-noun, 'claim' means 'lay claim to'; with a dependent clause it can mean 'assert'; avoid using it as substitute for 'declare', 'maintain', or 'charge'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'declared', 'maintained', 'charged' for those senses; in many contexts 'claimed to be' is better than 'claimed that'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clever (overused)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Clever' is overused and is best restricted to ingenuity displayed in small matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more precise descriptors for notable achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare (to/with distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Compare to' points out resemblances between different orders; 'compare with' points out differences between similar orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'compare to' for metaphorical analogies and 'compare with' for comparisons of similar things. Examples: life compared to a pilgrimage; Congress compared with British Parliament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: When meaning 'believe to be', 'consider' is not followed by 'as' (e.g., 'I consider him competent'). When meaning 'examine', 'consider' can be followed by 'as'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish meanings to avoid incorrect constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data (plural)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Data' is a plural noun like 'phenomena' or 'strata'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plural agreement: 'These data were tabulated.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependable
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Dependable' is a needless substitute for 'reliable' or 'trustworthy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'reliable' or 'trustworthy' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different than
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Different than' is not permissible; use 'different from', 'other than', or 'unlike'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'different than' with standard alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divided into (vs composed of)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Divided into' should not be misused for 'composed of'; line is sometimes difficult: plays are 'divided into' acts, poems are 'composed of' stanzas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term appropriate to the structure in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't (contraction usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contraction of 'do not'; the contraction of 'does not' is 'doesn't'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate contraction forms in informal contexts; avoid in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due to (correct vs incorrect uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Due to' is incorrectly used for 'through', 'because of', or 'owing to' in adverbial phrases; correct when related as predicate or modifier to a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'due to' only when it modifies a noun ('This invention is due to Edison') or in predicates ('losses due to preventable fires'). Otherwise use 'because of' or 'owing to'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folk (collective noun)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Folk' as a collective noun is equivalent to 'people' and should be used in singular form only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'folk' only in singular collective senses; prefer 'people' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect (noun vs verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a noun 'effect' means 'result'; as a verb it means 'to bring about' (not to be confused with 'affect' which means 'to influence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loose, vague uses of 'effect' in artistic criticism; prefer precise wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etc. (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Etc.' is equivalent to 'and the rest' and should not be used if it leaves the reader in doubt; least objectionable when representing the last terms of a previously given list or immaterial words at the end of a quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'etc.' at the end of a list introduced by 'such as' or 'for example'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (use only for verifiable matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Fact' should be used only for matters capable of direct verification, not for judgments or conclusions of taste or evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'fact' for verifiable events or properties; do not call subjective conclusions 'facts'. See also guidance about 'the fact that' under Rule 13.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (hackneyed word)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Factor' is hackneyed and usually replaceable by more direct idiomatic phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace with clearer phrasing that specifies the causal mechanism or role (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature (hackneyed word)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Feature' often adds nothing and is overused; as a verb in advertising sense (offer as special attraction) should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific: describe what the 'feature' actually is or how it was performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix (colloquial)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Fix' is colloquial in American English for 'arrange', 'prepare', 'mend'; restrict in writing to literary senses like 'fasten', 'make firm'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In formal writing prefer 'arrange', 'prepare', 'repair' rather than 'fix'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get (colloquial 'have got')
rubrics_metrics.description: The colloquial 'have got' for 'have' should not be used in writing; prefer 'have' and 'got' as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple forms; the preferable form of the participle is 'got'.

rubrics_metrics.name: He is a man who (redundant construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common redundant expression; often better to state the quality directly ('He is very ambitious') rather than 'He is a man who is very ambitious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'a man/woman who' constructions when unnecessary; recast sentences to be more direct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help (usage with 'but')
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'But' entry — misuse after 'help' ('could not help see but that' etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct gerundial or infinitive forms (e.g., 'could not help seeing that').

rubrics_metrics.name: However (positioning and meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: When meaning 'nevertheless', 'however' should not come first in the sentence or clause; when first it means 'in whatever way' or 'to whatever extent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place 'however' after an introductory element when it means 'nevertheless' (e.g., 'At last, however, we succeeded...'). Examples show literal uses 'However you advise him...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interesting (avoid perfunctory use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'interesting' as a perfunctory introduction; instead make the material interesting by presenting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not announce that what follows is interesting — show it. Recast or tell the anecdote without preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kind of (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'kind of' as substitute for 'rather' (before adjectives/verbs) or 'something like' (before nouns) except in familiar style; restrict to literal sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise modifiers rather than 'kind of' except in informal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less (fewer vs less)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Less' should not be misused for 'fewer' — 'less' refers to quantity, 'fewer' to number; exceptions for collective amounts exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'fewer' with countable nouns, 'less' with quantities; examples and edge cases provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Like (not to be used for 'as')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Like' governs nouns/pronouns; before phrases and clauses the equivalent word is 'as'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'as' before clauses: 'He thought as I did', not 'He thought like I did.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Line, along these lines (overused phrase)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Line' meaning 'course of procedure, conduct, thought' is allowable but overworked especially in phrase 'along these lines' and should be discarded for freshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clearer paraphrases: 'to the same effect', 'French literature' rather than 'along the line of French literature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal, literally (avoid exaggeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often incorrectly used to support exaggeration or violent metaphor ('literally dead with fatigue').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use literal/literally only for true literal senses; otherwise use accurate figurative language without 'literally'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lose out (colloquial and weak)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Lose out' is intended emphatic but less effective due to commonness; similar issues with 'try out', 'win out', 'sign up'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stronger, clearer verbs; recognize idiomatic 'out'/'up' combinations where meaning differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most (not = almost)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Most' should not be used to mean 'almost' (e.g., 'Most everybody' → 'Almost everybody').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'almost' when meaning nearly all; reserve 'most' for majority contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature (redundant usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Nature' often redundant when used like 'character'; used vaguely in phrases like 'lover of nature'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about what 'nature' refers to (scenery, rural life, wildlife, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Near by (adverbial phrase)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Near by' as an adverbial phrase is not fully accepted; 'near' or 'near at hand' is preferable; as adjective use 'neighboring'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'near' or 'neighboring' as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oftentimes, ofttimes (archaic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archaic forms no longer in good use; modern word is 'often'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'often'.

rubrics_metrics.name: One hundred and one (retain 'and')
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain 'and' in such expressions in accordance with traditional English usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'one hundred and one' rather than 'one hundred one'.

rubrics_metrics.name: One of the most (overused opening formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning essays or paragraphs with threadbare formulas like 'One of the most interesting developments...'; also ensure subject-verb agreement in following relative clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek fresher openings and correct relative-clause agreement ('One of the ablest men that have attacked this problem').

rubrics_metrics.name: Participle for verbal noun (gerund possessive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use possessive before a gerund when the actor is the subject of the gerund (e.g., 'Do you mind my asking a question?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the possessive with gerunds to avoid ambiguity; recast when possessive is awkward. Examples illustrate logical distinctions and safe practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: People vs The people
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The people' is a political term distinct from 'the public'; use appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'the people' for political sense (source of political support); 'the public' for artistic appreciation or patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase (meaning precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Phase' means a stage of transition and should not be used for 'aspect' or 'topic'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'point' or 'question' where appropriate rather than 'phase'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possess (do not substitute for have/own)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Possess' should not be used as a mere substitute for 'have' or 'own'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'have', 'own', or more natural phrasing: 'He had great courage' instead of 'He possessed great courage.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove (past participle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The past participle of 'prove' is 'proved'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'proved' rather than 'proven' in standard contexts for past participle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respective, respectively (often omit)
rubrics_metrics.description: These words may usually be omitted with advantage and their omission often improves clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary use; in some formal contexts (e.g., geometric proofs) they may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shall, Will (future-tense usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional rule: 'shall' for first person future, 'will' for second and third; 'I shall' expresses belief about future action, 'I will' expresses determination or consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe traditional distinctions when appropriate to tone and formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Should (see 'Would')
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-reference to guidance on 'Would'; subtle modal usage distinctions implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow modal usage rules for 'should' versus 'would' as contextualized.

rubrics_metrics.name: So (avoid as intensifier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'so' as an intensifier in writing ('so good'); also see Rule 4 for 'so' introducing clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stronger adjectives or adverbs instead of 'so' for emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sort of (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'Kind of' entry — avoid as imprecise substitute except in familiar style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split infinitive (preferred avoidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though historically attested, splitting 'to' + infinitive with an adverb is in disfavor and avoided by careful writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'to inquire diligently' → 'to diligently inquire' avoided; choose un-split constructions for formal prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: State (do not substitute for say)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'State' should not be used as a mere substitute for 'say' or 'remark'; restrict to 'express fully or clearly'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'state' when meaning full or clear expression; otherwise use 'say' or 'remark'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student Body (avoid awkward phrase)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Student body' is a needless and awkward expression meaning 'students'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'a student'/'the students' or other simpler constructions (e.g., 'The students passed resolutions').

rubrics_metrics.name: System (avoid unnecessary use)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'System' is frequently used without need; prefer more direct phrasing ('government by commission' rather than 'commission system of government').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simpler nouns that convey meaning directly ('Dormitories' rather than 'the dormitory system').

rubrics_metrics.name: Thanking You in Advance (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'Thanking you in advance' sounds presumptuous; instead phrase requests politely and, if needed, send acknowledgment later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Will you please' or 'I shall be obliged' for requests; avoid anticipatory thanks.

rubrics_metrics.name: They (pronoun number agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using plural 'they' with singular distributive antecedents (each, everybody, anyone) — traditionally use 'he' unless antecedent is or must be feminine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'he' with distributive nouns per traditional usage or recast to avoid gendered pronouns; note modern alternatives exist but guidance here favors 'he'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very (use sparingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'very' sparingly; where emphasis is necessary, prefer words strong in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose inherently stronger adjectives/adverbs instead of leaning on 'very'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewpoint (use 'point of view')
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 'point of view' rather than misusing 'viewpoint' for 'view' or 'opinion'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terms accurately to avoid imprecision.

rubrics_metrics.name: While (avoid indiscriminate substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'while' indiscriminately for 'and', 'but', or 'although'; 'while' properly means 'during the time that' or, with strict literalness, 'at the same time'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace with semicolon or the appropriate connective where 'while' is used to mean 'and'/'but'. 'While' is allowable as 'although' where it causes no ambiguity; otherwise prefer 'although' or 'at the same time'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whom (correct subject/object usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Whom' is often incorrectly used for 'who' before 'he said' etc. when it is really the subject of a following verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'who' when the clause that follows has 'who' as subject; use 'whom' when functioning as object. Examples provided for common confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worth while (avoid overworked approval phrase)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Worth while' is overworked as vague approval or, with 'not', disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more precise terms of evaluation rather than the vague 'worth while' or its negative.
